title: A visual-cortex prosthesis that restores useful, detailed sight

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an implanted system that translates external visual information, such as camera input, into stimulation of the visual cortex that a person can use as detailed, practical sight. Its goal is a stable visual representation that supports everyday activities, including navigation, recognizing faces and reading. This would require much more than eliciting isolated points of light, known as phosphenes, or recognizable simple shapes.

The system would combine a durable brain interface with a method for encoding visual information into spatial and temporal stimulation patterns. Translating camera input is a system-level formulation of the encoding challenge; the supplied evidence does not establish a camera-to-cortex pipeline that already delivers this level of sight. The intended capability remains hypothetical.

significance.text: If achieved, useful cortical vision could restore access to visual information for some people whose eyes or optic nerves cannot transmit it. Independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading would represent a major restorative advance because stimulation would convey information directly to brain circuits downstream of the failed transmission pathway. These benefits depend on effective visual encoding and safe, durable stimulation; they have not been demonstrated at the proposed level in the supplied record.

Mechanistic synthesis: this approach would depend on surviving visual circuits that can respond to stimulation and support useful perception. That is a reasoned boundary on the concept, rather than an established clinical eligibility rule in the supplied evidence. Extensive destruction of the necessary circuits would require additional restorative advances. Bypassing damaged upstream structures does not by itself repair those structures or recreate all the functions of natural vision.

Conditional downstream possibilities include greater independence in travel, communication, education and work. Their extent would depend on the information the prosthesis actually conveys, training requirements and performance outside controlled settings. Success on selected tasks would not establish natural visual acuity, a natural visual field or suitability for every cause of blindness.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is a reliable mapping from visual information to stimulation, neural activity and useful perception. The July 2025 perspective identifies understanding the relationship between stimulation, neural activity and behavior as a critical hurdle. Evoking percepts establishes that cortical stimulation can produce visual experiences, but does not establish how to construct a stable, detailed scene from them. Spatial and temporal stimulation patterns must convey information that recipients can interpret consistently.

Resolution and visual-field coverage must improve together. Fine stimulation over a small cortical region does not automatically provide a broad usable field, while broader stimulation does not automatically preserve detail. Increasing stimulation intensity also encounters tissue-safety constraints: the perspective identifies tissue-damage risks from high currents. A successful interface must therefore achieve useful precision and coverage within safe stimulation limits.

Durability is a separate engineering and biological barrier. The perspective describes chronic variability in stimulation thresholds and adverse tissue responses, which can undermine a consistent relationship between device settings and perception. An interface must remain effective over time while limiting tissue injury, and its encoding must remain usable as the interface and its interaction with tissue change. These are documented barriers in the 2025 account; the supplied record does not establish their subsequent resolution or persistence through November 2026.

current_state.text: Kim and colleagues’ perspective, “Towards precise synthetic neural codes: high-dimensional stimulation with flexible electrodes,” published on 14 July 2025, describes human shape perception using dynamically steered surface stimulation of the visual cortex. It also reports shape perception in monkeys using patterned stimulation through 14 Utah electrode arrays implanted in primary visual cortex, V1. These reports provide a technical basis for patterned cortical visual stimulation, but do not demonstrate independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading through a detailed cortical visual scene.

The perspective identifies inadequate resolution, limited visual-field coverage and stimulation safety as major limitations. Its discussion also connects the broader prospects for neural stimulation to chronic interface stability and the difficulty of mapping stimulation to behavior. The evidence therefore supports a progression from evoked phosphenes toward shape perception, while leaving the proposed practical-sight capability unestablished.

These experimental descriptions come from the perspective as assessed in the supplied review, rather than independent examination of its cited experiments. The review notes that reference 112 concerns cochlear implants and is misplaced as visual evidence; the perspective’s explicit narrative and reference 38 still support its account of human shape perception. This citation problem limits reliance on that particular reference and does not establish that the reported human result is false.

The supplied review reports complete extraction of the perspective’s main text and references, with no indicated truncation or extraction problems. Its conclusions about shapes, coverage and safety were based on text and did not require inspection of figures. Nevertheless, this is a July 2025 account: the supplied record contains no subsequent search evidence establishing the field’s status through 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional demonstration: people with otherwise untreatable blindness independently use an implanted system for navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading across varied real-world settings. Evaluation should specify participant characteristics, task difficulty, assistance allowed and performance thresholds before testing. These are proposed criteria for making “useful, detailed sight” concrete, rather than published consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading across real-world settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attribution and reproducibility requirements: controlled comparisons should establish how much performance depends on the device’s visual input, accounting for residual vision, memorized environments and nonvisual cues. Results should reproduce across participants, sessions and unfamiliar settings, with independent replication where feasible. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth across those conditions, not universal performance in every environment or for every form of blindness.
completion_criteria.label: Visual-input-dependent performance reproduces across participants, sessions and unfamiliar settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and safety requirements: follow-up over years should establish whether useful performance persists, how stimulation thresholds and calibration needs change, and whether neurological or tissue harms remain within prospectively defined acceptable limits. A convincing protocol would specify follow-up duration, adverse-event limits, device failures and maintenance requirements. Years of durability are an intended demonstration target, not a duration validated by the supplied source.
completion_criteria.label: Useful performance persists for years within predefined safety limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report achieved visual detail, field coverage and everyday task performance alongside training burden, dependence on assistance and conditions in which the device fails. These measurements should make clear whether success represents a limited but useful visual aid or the broader detailed-sight capability proposed here. Participant selection should also make explicit the condition of the surviving visual pathways and cortex, without assuming that one successful group establishes suitability for all causes of blindness.
completion_criteria.label: Report visual capabilities, practical burdens and participant suitability limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: NRL-16, “Biologically repair the injured visual pathway,” shares the goal of restoring vision but proposes biological repair, whereas NRL-08 supplies visual information through cortical stimulation. The approaches could be complementary. Only NRL-16’s title is supplied, so the record does not establish which injuries it addresses or whether it could repair extensive destruction of visual brain circuits.

Roster-based comparison: NRL-17, “A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation,” overlaps in long-term tissue compatibility, stimulation reliability and conveying sensory information to the nervous system. NRL-08 has the specific endpoint of useful cortical sight; NRL-17 has a broader movement-and-sensation interface goal. NRL-07, “A dependable neural communication channel for profound paralysis,” also concerns reliable neural interfaces, but its stated endpoint is communication rather than visual restoration.

Roster-based comparison: NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation,” could inform how stimulation produces meaningful neural activity. NRL-03, “Whole-brain, cellular-resolution recording during natural behavior,” could provide research capabilities relevant to understanding circuit responses. Neither title establishes a prerequisite for cortical visual prostheses: practical encoding might advance without a general theory or whole-brain recording.

Roster-based comparison: NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” addresses a different problem that may become relevant when necessary brain circuits have been destroyed. NRL-08 primarily seeks to use surviving circuits through an implanted interface. Replacing tissue and restoring cortical visual input remain distinct innovations, and the supplied roster does not establish that either would solve the other’s barriers.

change_log.reason: The review supports these specific experimental details and their different species and interface scopes.

change_log.change: Integrated the encoding, simultaneous resolution-and-coverage, stimulation-safety and chronic interface-stability barriers.
change_log.reason: These complementary scientific and engineering distinctions explain why shape perception does not establish useful, detailed sight.

change_log.change: Qualified recipient suitability and downstream benefits as mechanistic reasoning and conditional possibilities.
change_log.reason: The source does not establish clinical eligibility rules, outcomes by blindness etiology or the proposed everyday benefits.

change_log.reason: The final inputs include NRL-16’s title but no detailed scope or evidence supporting that stronger relationship.

unresolved_issues: Developments after July 2025, including the field’s status through 1 November 2026, are not established by the supplied record.
The underlying human and monkey experiments were not independently assessed in the supplied review; their detailed protocols, participant scope and performance measures remain outside this record.
The relationship between blindness etiology, surviving visual circuitry and suitability for cortical prostheses remains unspecified.
Task thresholds, participant criteria, follow-up duration, acceptable adverse-event limits and practical maintenance requirements need a prospective evaluation protocol.
NRL-16’s detailed scope remains unavailable. The recommendation to remove the unsupported circuit-repair assertion was adopted; its roster title supports only a broad comparison.

brief.title: Useful, detailed sight through a brain implant
possible: Some people whose eyes or optic nerves can no longer carry visual information could navigate independently, recognize faces and read ordinary text. A camera would send information to an implant that stimulates the visual cortex, the brain region that processes sight.
why: Restoring access to visual information could give people greater independence in travel, communication, education and work. The implant would deliver information directly to the brain, bypassing the damaged pathway from the eyes.

sources.who: Robin Kim and colleagues at Rice University
sources.showed: Their perspective reviews how patterned brain stimulation can produce recognizable shapes. Their computer simulation found that independently controlled stimulation sites produced more varied brain activity.
sources.quote: Single-channel stimulation activates the entire cortical column, resulting in highly synchronized, low-dimensional neural activity.
sources.cited_for: The work explains why precise stimulation across space and time matters for artificial sight.
sources.not_established: The simulation and reviewed shape experiments do not establish detailed, practical sight.

sources.who: Michael P. Barry, Philip R. Troyk and collaborators
sources.showed: This preprint reports camera-guided visual benefits in a blind participant whose wireless implants remained functional for over three years. A heat-sensing camera reduced distracting visual information.
sources.quote:
Counterintuitively, pausing camera-based stimulation 
during more than half of each second improved performance.
sources.cited_for: Wireless implants can support camera-guided visual tasks and remain functional over years.
sources.not_established: The small feasibility study does not demonstrate detailed scenes, face recognition or ordinary reading across everyday settings.

sources.who: Fabrizio Grani, Eduardo Fernandez and collaborators
sources.showed: In two blind volunteers, recorded brain activity predicted whether stimulation produced perceived flashes of light, called phosphenes, and how bright they appeared.
sources.quote: our results indicate that subjective visual experience can be accurately predicted from the recorded neural activity.
sources.cited_for: Brain recordings could help relate stimulation settings to what a recipient perceives.
sources.not_established: Predicting isolated flashes does not establish automatic control of a stable, detailed visual scene.

sources.showed: A blind participant identified some letters and recognized object boundaries through stimulation from implanted electrodes, the small contacts that deliver electrical pulses.
sources.quote: Implantation and subsequent explantation of intracortical microelectrodes were carried out without complications.
sources.cited_for: Implanted contacts can produce distinguishable visual patterns in a blind person.
sources.not_established: Recognizing selected letters and boundaries does not establish ordinary reading or long-term safety.

sources.who: Michael S. Beauchamp, Daniel Yoshor and collaborators
sources.showed: Blind and sighted participants recognized letter shapes when electrical stimulation traced them across the brain’s visual map.
sources.quote:
In both sighted and blind participants, dynamic stimulation enabled accurate
recognition of letter shapes predicted by the brain’s spatial map of the visual world.
sources.cited_for: The order and timing of stimulation can turn separate flashes into recognizable forms.
sources.not_established: Recognizing traced forms does not establish a continuously updated view of everyday surroundings.

shown: Barry and collaborators report the closest step toward practical use: camera-guided visual tasks with wireless implants functioning for over three years in a blind participant. This preprint shows limited visual benefits, rather than complex scenes.

Beauchamp’s and Fernández’s teams have produced recognizable shapes or selected letters through brain stimulation. Grani’s team linked brain recordings to perceived flashes, offering a way to measure what stimulation produces.
missing: No system has demonstrated independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading together across varied everyday settings.
A reliable way to turn camera images into stable, detailed perceptions across a broad field of view remains missing.
Useful sight must persist as tissue responses and stimulation needs change, without unacceptable harm.

milestones.label: Independent navigation, face recognition and ordinary reading
milestones.explanation: People with otherwise untreatable blindness would have to perform these activities across varied real-world settings under predefined test conditions. This would establish practical, detailed sight.

milestones.label: Visual input drives repeatable performance across people and settings
milestones.explanation: Controlled tests would have to isolate the visual input’s contribution and reproduce benefits across people, sessions and unfamiliar settings. This would distinguish useful vision from memory or other cues.

milestones.label: Useful sight persists safely for years
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to show sustained performance within predefined safety limits while tracking changing stimulation needs, failures and maintenance. This would establish whether the benefit can last.

milestones.label: Visual abilities, daily burdens and suitability limits are clear
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to report visual detail, field coverage, task performance, training, assistance, failures and participant suitability. This would define the aid’s practical scope and who could benefit.

uncertain: Which causes of blindness leave enough working visual circuitry for the implant to help remains unclear.
The performance thresholds, follow-up length and acceptable harms needed to judge success remain unsettled.
It remains unclear how much training, recalibration and assistance everyday use would require.

page.title: Cortical prosthesis for reading, face recognition and navigation
page.definition: An implanted cortical visual prosthesis converts camera images into electrical stimulation of the visual cortex, the brain tissue that processes vision. Blind recipients use the resulting perceptions for continuous-text reading, face recognition and navigation in everyday environments.

goal.need: WHO’s estimates of unaddressed distance vision impairment or blindness include millions of people with glaucoma or diabetic retinopathy. Cortical prostheses are being developed to bypass damaged eyes and optic nerves and deliver camera-derived signals directly to the visual cortex.

figures.caption: Unaddressed distance vision impairment or blindness attributed to two causes.
figures.note: Estimates quoted in WHO’s fact sheet dated 10 February 2026. These include vision impairment and blindness; they do not estimate eligibility for cortical implantation.

statements.quote: to help people with ocular causes of blindness regain at least some functional vision.
statements.context: NEI describes the purpose of its supported research on the Orion cortical visual prosthesis.

statements.quote: The goal is useful visual perception: spots or patterns of light that may support orientation and visual tasks rather than recreate normal sight.
The goal of this work is to address fundamental questions that will allow the development of a Smart Bionic Eye
statements.context: The NIH-funded registered study names face recognition, outdoor navigation, reading and self-care as target tasks. It includes users of cortical and retinal prostheses.

completion.title: Blind recipients read text, recognise faces and navigate using cortical prosthetic vision in daily life.
completion.criterion: The same blind recipients use an implanted, camera-driven cortical visual prosthesis to read continuous text, recognise faces and navigate in everyday environments. A registered clinical study establishes benefit attributable to visual input against device-off and appropriate control conditions, using its prespecified task, safety and follow-up criteria. This is an Atlas fallback: no common reading speed, face-recognition accuracy, navigation score or follow-up duration defines this combined capability.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, drawing the task set from NCT06117332 and the natural-environment requirement from HOVER; no outside body located defines the combined completion test.
completion.basis: Searches of HOVER recommendations, FDA retinal-prosthesis guidance, cortical-prosthesis trial records and Cortigent filings found no completion threshold combining these functions. The task set follows the Smart Bionic Eye programme. HOVER identifies “a benefit in the natural environment” as the goal. Selected-letter recognition and positive low-vision assessments do not establish the combined capability.

milestones.title: A cortical visual prosthesis obtains FDA authorisation for its first human investigation.
milestones.criterion: FDA permits a first-in-human investigation after reviewing the cortical visual prosthesis’s prior investigations and investigational plan. Preclinical evidence is device-specific; there is no universal animal-survival cutoff. Surface electrodes: Cortigent’s filing describes the six-person Orion early feasibility study. Intracortical electrodes: Troyk’s 2020 symposium abstract describes preclinical safety testing accepted for an FDA-authorised ICVP study.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 812.20; this milestone concerns the US investigational-device pathway.
milestones.threshold_quote: A sponsor shall not begin an investigation for which FDA's approval of an application is required until FDA has approved the application.

milestones.title: A cortical visual prosthesis elicits light percepts with a measurable detection threshold in a blind person.
milestones.criterion: Stimulation produces phosphenes, perceived flashes of light, with a measurable detection threshold. The cited intracortical protocol defines threshold at 50% detection and includes sham trials. Intracortical electrodes: one blind participant detected 947/1,000 stimuli, with 23/500 sham false positives over four days; 88/96 electrodes evoked phosphenes. Surface electrodes: Beauchamp et al. mapped stimulation-evoked phosphenes in two blind participants.
milestones.set_by: CORTIVIS investigators, published stimulation protocol in Fernández et al. (2021). The quoted 50% definition was used for intracortical electrodes; measurable phosphene detection is also used with surface electrodes.

milestones.title: Blind recipients distinguish electrically evoked visual forms above the task’s chance level.
milestones.criterion: Recipients discriminate electrically evoked forms above the chance rate of the forced-choice task. Surface electrodes: one blind participant identified 33/36 three-choice forms, 92% versus 33% chance, at 30 forms/minute. Intracortical electrodes: one blind participant distinguished selected letter pairs with greater than 70% accuracy in 24 sessions over five days, versus 50% chance. These results concern selected forms rather than continuous-text reading.
milestones.set_by: Visual psychophysics convention applied in Beauchamp et al. (2020) and Fernández et al. (2021): forced-choice discrimination exceeding chance. The quotation is from the intracortical study.
milestones.threshold_quote: The subject’s performance was always above chance level

milestones.title: Camera-driven cortical stimulation improves visually guided tasks relative to device-off performance.
milestones.criterion: Camera-driven stimulation improves a visually guided task under device-on versus device-off comparison using the published study’s analysis. Intracortical electrodes: one participant approached a person successfully in 17/20 thermal-camera trials versus 8/20 without stimulation, P < 0.01. Surface electrodes: four Orion recipients had positive or mildly positive home-based Functional Low-Vision Observer Rated Assessment results at 36 months. The ICVP preprint and company-reported Orion results are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Controlled functional-vision comparisons used by the ICVP and Orion investigators; HOVER recommends assessment with and without prosthetic input. The quoted result concerns intracortical stimulation.
milestones.threshold_quote: Participant 1 showed significant improvement for most tasks with camera-driven stimulation.

milestones.title: A cortical visual prosthesis still elicits visual perceptions at 72 months after implantation.
milestones.criterion: Visual perceptions remain elicitable at the Orion protocol’s 72-month assessment; adverse events are evaluated across six years. The registry specifies no minimum functioning-electrode fraction or acceptable adverse-event rate. Surface electrodes: three of six Orion participants completed six-year visits; functioning implants were reported, but a complete electrode-level 72-month perception result was not found. Intracortical electrodes: 366/400 ICVP electrodes remained electrically reliable on day 1351 in one participant. The company results and ICVP preprint are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Second Sight Medical Products, NCT03344848 secondary visual-perception endpoint. The 72-month assessment is specified in the outcome table; this duration was published for the surface-electrode Orion system.

milestones.title: A clinical study meets its endpoints for cortical-prosthesis reading, face recognition and navigation.
milestones.criterion: A registered study of an implanted camera-driven cortical visual prosthesis meets its prespecified efficacy endpoints for continuous-text reading, face recognition and navigation in the same recipients, together with its safety endpoint. This stage concerns controlled clinical testing before demonstration in everyday environments. No qualifying result was identified for either electrode placement; no published combined endpoint or numerical pass criterion was found.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback. Searches of cortical-prosthesis trial records, HOVER, FDA retinal-prosthesis guidance and Cortigent filings found no published combined clinical success criterion. The activities follow the Smart Bionic Eye programme.

not_found: No public Orion pivotal-trial protocol defining numerical safety and efficacy success criteria was found.
ClinicalTrials.gov study pages rendered without study text; indexed versions of the primary registry records were accessible.
No shared cortical-prosthesis threshold for reading speed, face-recognition accuracy, navigation performance or acceptable adverse-event frequency was found.

results.detail: The study defined threshold at approximately 63% detection.

Single-electrode

ranging 4.8–59 μA (0.97–12 nC/phase) with mean (–standard deviation, SD) 29–12 μA (5.8–2.4

results.finding: One blind participant distinguished horizontal and vertical gratings with 90% accuracy.
results.detail: The two-choice task had a 50% chance level; results covered spatial frequencies of 0.04–0.15 cycles per degree.
results.quote:
Participant 2’s performance with stimulation was consistently 90% correct (combined 95% CI: 
77–96%) across 0.04–0.15 cpd (P < 0.03 for 0.15 cpd, binomial test).

results.finding: One blind participant approached a person successfully in 17 of 20 thermal-camera trials.
results.detail: Success was 8/20 without stimulation; the reported permutation test gave P < 0.01.

Participant 1 was successful in 
8/20 trials (40%, 95% CI: 22–61%) with no stimulation, 11/20 trials (55%, 95% CI: 34–74%)
